summary: Supply number of successes, the probability of success, the mean and the subject of continuity correction and the Continuity correction calculator solves for number of trials (N). It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Continuity correction calculator work?
sections.html:
The Continuity correction calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of trials (N) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in number of successes (n), the probability of success (0<p<1), the mean (μ) and the subject of continuity correction.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Continuity correction calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of trials (N)=mean (μ) ÷ probability of success (0<p<1)
Standard deviation (σ)=(the square root of ((number of trials (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × (1 − probability of success (0<p<1)))))
Variance (σ²)=(number of trials (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × (1 − probability of success (0<p<1)))
Z-score=(number of successes (n), mean (μ), (the square root of ((number of trials (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × (1 − probability of success (0<p<1))))), var sub)
Z-value=((number of successes (n), mean (μ), (the square root of ((number of trials (N) × probability of success (0<p<1) × (1 − probability of success (0<p<1))))), var sub))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Continuity correction calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — number of successes, the probability of success and the mean — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Continuity correction calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of trials (N), derived from number of successes, the probability of success and the mean. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Continuity correction calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of successes, the probability of success, the mean and the subject of continuity correction, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Continuity correction calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
